source.title: When Style Breaks Safety: Defending Language Models Against Superficial Style Alignment
source.authors: Yu-Xin Xiao; Sana Tonekaboni; Walter Gerych; Vinith M. Suriyakumar; M. Ghassemi

record.file_problem: none; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign instruction fine-tuning increases harmful-request compliance, using style-specific fine-tuning and ASR rather than the original study’s recipe.
record.gate_note: The paper directly tests benign fine-tuning and harmful-query ASR (V2). It does not test harmful-example fine-tuning, first-token KL concentration, compliant-opening or decoding bypasses, safety localization in weights, why safety is shallow, or whether deepening safety fixes the issue. Style-pattern prompt comparisons and the controlled synthetic-style evaluation are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not test one of the listed versions. Cited results and utility-only measures are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-aligned instruct models (Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, gemma-3-12b; also DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in the appendix) on benign data with no safety examples. It measures harmful-query ASR before and after, on style-controlled sets (1,000 or 10,000 examples) and on real-world Dolly-15K and Alpaca-52K. That is a different recipe aimed at the same V2 question.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is largely right. To add: the authors report that benign fine-tuning raised ASR across all training and testing styles, consistent with Qi et al. (2024). The matched-style rise is attributed to semantic style compliance rather than token-level triggers. SafeStyle (50 style-matched safety examples) beats baselines, including Constrained, at preserving safety.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign supervised instruction fine-tuning and harmful-query ASR, as in the broader fine-tuning safety question, but studies style-specific tuning, typically at 1,000 or 10,000 examples or on real-world datasets; it does not test harmful fine-tuning or the original few-to-hundreds-example recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR changes with fine-tuning style, whether training and test styles match, proportion of style-removed data, dataset and model; style-pattern position has little effect. ASR inflation prompt comparisons were also checked across judges.

fits_no_version.finding: Semantically irrelevant style patterns in jailbreak queries raise ASR in 32 of 36 models (paired t-test p = 0.0002).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Style phrasing in harmful requests increases harmful compliance relative to the bare intent.

fits_no_version.finding: Six synthetic styles each raise ASR; Shakespearean style has the largest effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Specific response-style requests independently raise harmful compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: ASR inflation correlates with attention to style tokens versus intent tokens (Spearman 0.456). ASR-inflating styles have higher bigram overlap with OLMo's instruction-tuning data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-exposure to a style in alignment data makes models comply with harmful queries in that style.

record.problems: ASR is judged by LLMs; the paper reports checks with alternative judges. Main Figure 4 values are plotted without numerical values in the text. The authors report means across three runs but no error bars for those runs in the supplied results. The paper notes it lacks access to other proprietary alignment datasets.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded No Defense-independent defense strategy results in Tables 1 and 2 because they compare the paper’s defense methods rather than isolate the benign fine-tuning effect; excluded LC WR utility outcomes. Figure 4 rows retain the matched-style conditions and mixture ratios but not every non-matched test-style curve or every epoch value, which is figure-only. No additional separate benchmark-level rows were extracted from Figure 2 because the text supplies only aggregate counts for the directly relevant style-prompt effect.

untested.parts: No few-example (10–100) benign fine-tuning; the smallest set is 1,000 examples. No closed-model or API fine-tuning.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding attacks. Style phrasing in queries is a different manipulation.
No weight or rank localization. SPPFT (freezing safety layers) appears only as a defense baseline.
Does not test why safety is shallow in early tokens. It offers a different mechanism: style-intent association.
No deepening data-augmentation training. The Constrained baseline (Qi et al. 2025a's token-wise constrained objective) appears only as a comparison defense; see missing.

missing.what: Diverse-style (original Alpaca) training curves in Figure 4: smallest overall ASR increase. Also cross-style spillover: list-trained models show the largest increase, including on other test styles.
News-prefix and legal-prefix 1,000-example fine-tuning on Llama-3.1-8B: ASR rises most when train and test styles match.
No Defense ΔASR on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B: news +0.063, legal +0.013 (weak).
No Defense ΔASR on original (unstyled) queries after style tuning on Llama: news +0.008 (near zero), legal +0.523.
Alternative-judge No Defense ΔASR for Llama (Llama-Guard and Qwen3Guard), e.g. legal +0.589/+0.630 and Shakespeare +0.162/+0.154, consistent with GPT-4o.
Semantic versus syntactic trigger test: paraphrased list-style jailbreaks still raise ASR, while syntactic overlap alone raises it much less.

Constrained baseline (Qi et al. 2025a's token-wise constrained fine-tuning) under benign fine-tuning. ΔASR is near zero in most settings but +0.267 for gemma Shakespeare. LC WR gains are often lower, e.g. Qwen legal +11.5 vs +29.1 for No Defense.
missing.versions: V7 (arguably: durability of the original paper's fine-tuning-time defense)

record.verdict_notes: The study is not one of the originals. Verdicts rest on the No Defense rows; defense-comparison rows are correctly excluded. Shakespeare-style baseline ASR is high for the original models, which may explain the Qwen reversal. Figure 4 rows are figure-only, so their states rely on the authors' text. The 0%:100% rows duplicate one model. Whether the Constrained baseline counts as a V7 test is debatable: it protects early-token alignment during fine-tuning rather than deepening it. So no V7 verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and whether a few to a few hundred harmful examples remove refusal.

Does not test ordinary benign fine-tuning without the study’s style manipulations at few-example scale; the main controlled study uses 1,000 instructions, and other fine-tuning settings use 10,000 instructions or real-world datasets.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefilled compliant openings, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes; the tested style phrasing is not these bypass interventions.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or the training objective causes safety to be shallow in the first response tokens.
Whether training spreads safety beyond early tokens and whether such deepening holds up.
